newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac defends Juppe from Gaullist sniping.
newsitem.headline: Chirac defends Juppe from Gaullist sniping.

text.p: Embattled French Prime Minister Alain Juppe faced open dissent within his Gaullist RPR party on Thursday, prompting an angry President Jacques Chirac to intervene by telephone to support him.

Former premier Edouard Balladur hit out in a speech to Gaullist parliamentarians in Le Havre at two Juppe policy initiatives, voicing opposition to proposals for new anti-racism laws and changes in the electoral system.

Balladur's comments, which won applause, followed a blistering attack on the prime minister by back-bencher Etienne Garnier on Wednesday and a statement of "disapproval" by veteran Gaullist lawmaker Pierre Mazeaud.
RPR parliamentary floor leader Michel Pericard told reporters Chirac had telephoned him to express "indignation" at the attacks on the government.
Juppe has called a parliamentary confidence vote next Wednesday in an effort to unite his fractious centre-right coalition but this has done nothing to stop sniping.

Party officials said Garnier faced possible disciplinary action for calling Juppe an "irreparable prime minister...whose dogmatism and clumsiness are leading the country towards insurmountable problems and unacceptable inequality."

Balladur, defeated for the presidency by Chirac last year, said in his speech: "We will not respond to citizens' concerns by multiplying and refining our legal arsenal, nor by changing the election law at the risk of depriving the Fifth Republic of any stable majority."

Juppe, whose public approval rating has sunk to barely 30 percent, split his coalition by proposing a "dose" of proportional representation in the parliamentary voting system and a new anti-racism law to make it easier to prosecute extreme-right anti-immigration crusader Jean-Marie Le Pen.
The Union for French Democracy (UDF), junior partner in the coalition, criticised both ideas at its parliamentary conference earlier this week.

Balladur, who had shunned Gaullist meetings since his presidential defeat in May 1995, said he supported Juppe's government when it took unpopular decisions to cut public spending and bring down the budget deficit.

"But that is not enough. We must do more," he said. "This is all necessary but not sufficient to return quickly to growth and employment, we must go further and complete this with action on the fiscal, wage and monetary fronts."

RPR floor leader Michel Pericard hinted that Garnier could be de-selected by the party for his attack on Juppe. He told reporters that Garnier had "crossed the red line" and talked like a political adversary.

Noting that selection boards would start picking Gaullist candidates for the 1998 parliamentary elections next week, Pericard said: "Those who talk like our opponents will be treated by the voters like opponents. I don't think it will bring them good luck."
